source_text:
Praeclara quaedam res est silentium, tum aliis plerumque permultis, tum mihi nunc vel maxime, qui volens nolensque clausum os habeo, et tacere cogor. Inexercitatus enim sum ac plane rudis sermonum illorum elegantium atque ornatorum, qui selectis, probatisque nominibus ac verbis, perpetuo quodam et inoffenso ductu pronuntiantur aut componuntur: fortasse a natura ipsa ad venustum hoc, et vere Graecanicum opus elaborandum minus comparatus. Sed et octavus iam annus est, ex quo nec brevem, longamve orationem ullam habui ipse, nec aut scripsi; nec alium audivi quem vel privatim scribentem, historiamve, vel publice panegyricos sermones, controversiasque declamantem, praeter hosce admirabiles viros, qui pulchram philosophiam amplexi sunt: quibus scilicet elocutionis, elegantiaeque verborum cura minor est; postpositis autem vocibus, res ipsas, ut se habeant, accurate singulas investigare et enuntiare volunt: non quod alterum illud nolint, opinor; quin volunt quam maxime praeclaras, et accuratas cogitationes suas praeclaro et omnis mendacii experte sermone exprimere: sed quod fortasse non possint, nec adeo sic in promptu; hinc sacram ac divinam facultatem propriis explicare sententiis; hinc orationem verbis comptam atque concinnam adferre; et quae duorum hominum propria cuiusque est praerogativa, una et eadem, eaque parva et humana mente complecti; praesertim cum utriusque dispar ac penitus contraria sit ratio. Cogitationi siquidem, inventionique rerum amicum quodammodo, et consors operis est silentium: dicendi vero facultatem, et pronunciationis dignitatem haud alibi reperias, quam in verbis, verborumque assidua meditatione ac usu. Quin etiam et alia quaedam mentem disciplina vehementer occupat, et os linguam plane constringit, si vel exiguum quippiam Graeca voce eloqui velim: mirificae nimirum leges nostrae, quibus omnium nunc, qui Romanorum imperio parent, res gubernantur: quae quidem neque conduntur, neque percipiuntur sine labore ac molestia; et sapientes quidem illae, piaeque sunt et variae, et suspiciendae, atque ut uno verbo dicam, Graecissimae: ceterum Romano expositae, traditaeque sermone, admirabili sane atque magnifico, et ad imperii maiestatem confirmato; sed mihi gravi nihilominus ac difficili. Non enim aliter sentire aut posse aut velle me unquam dixerim. Cum autem aliud nihil sint voces nostrae, quam imagines quaedam animi nostri conceptuum ac notionum; iis quidem, qui dicendi facultate valent, tanquam pictoribus quibusdam et arte peritissimis, et colorum copia instructissimis, non similes modo, sed varias etiam, et ad speciem crebra florum admixtione pulcherrimas pingere licere sine ullo impedimento, confitendum est.

Nos vero, quasi pauperes quidam, variis huiusmodi fucis carentes, et qui vel nunquam eos in arte nostra habuerimus, vel eos fortasse abiecerimus; tanquam solis carbonibus aut testulis viratorum, communiumque nominum ac verborum, prima animi nostri sensa, iis quae supersunt vocibus depingentes effingimus; typorum animi characteres, si non claros, nec ad speciem ornatos; at quemadmodum in carbonum pictura fieri solet, quoquo modo representare conantes; si quid uspiam venustum ac disertum se offerat, sponte nostra, ut qui haec aspernemur, reicientes. Verum et tertium quiddam rursum aliud est, quod impedit, et avocat, et multo magis, quam cetera, nos retinet, silentioque uti iubet, argumentum nempe ipsum; de quo dicere auebam quidem, sed cunctari nunc cogor, et haereo. De viro enim dicere institui, qui homo quidem esse videtur, et talis apparet; iis vero, qui magnitudinem eius habitus, moresque intueri possunt, maioribus quibusdam ornamentis instructus ac prope divinis videatur.
english: Silence is a splendid thing — for many others in many cases, and for me now most of all. Willing or unwilling, I keep my mouth shut and am forced to be quiet. I am unpracticed and wholly raw in those elegant and ornate speeches that are uttered or composed with a continuous, unstumbling flow of chosen and approved names and words. Perhaps nature itself fitted me poorly for working out this graceful and truly Greek craft.

And already it is the eighth year since I myself have delivered any speech, short or long, or written one; nor have I heard anyone else either writing privately, or history, or publicly declaiming panegyric speeches and controversies — except these admirable men who have embraced the beautiful philosophy. For them the care of elocution and elegance of words is lesser. Setting words aside, they want to investigate and declare the things themselves, accurately and one by one, as they are. Not that they refuse the other gift, I think; rather they greatly desire to express their splendid and exact thoughts in a splendid speech free of every falsehood. But perhaps they cannot do both so readily: on the one hand to unfold the sacred and divine faculty in their own conceptions, and on the other to bring forward a speech trimmed and fitted in words — and to grasp, in one and the same little human mind, the prerogative proper to each of two men — especially since the manner of each is different and utterly contrary.

For silence is somehow the friend of thought and of finding things out, and a partner in the work. But the faculty of speaking, and the dignity of delivery, you will not find elsewhere than in words and in their constant meditation and use. Besides, another discipline occupies the mind fiercely and binds the mouth and tongue if I even want to say a little in the Greek voice: I mean our marvelous laws, by which the affairs of all who now obey the Roman Empire are governed. They are neither framed nor grasped without labor and trouble; and they are wise and pious and varied and to be respected — and, to say it in one word, most Greek. Yet they are set out and handed down in the Roman tongue, a speech wonderful and magnificent and fitted to the majesty of empire, but still heavy and hard for me. I would never say that I could or would feel otherwise.

And since our words are nothing else than certain images of the concepts and notions of our mind, it must be granted that those who have strength in the faculty of speaking may paint, like painters most skilled in art and richest in colors, not only likenesses but varied and, for beauty, most lovely pictures by a thick mixing of flowers — without any hindrance.

But we, like certain poor men lacking these various cosmetics — who either never had them in our craft, or perhaps threw them away — try to sketch the first senses of our mind with charcoal alone, or with the potsherds of common names and words, painting with whatever voices remain. We fashion the characters of the mind's types, if not clear or adorned for show, then as charcoal pictures are made, trying somehow to represent them; and if anything graceful and eloquent offers itself, we reject it of our own will, as people who scorn such things.

Yet there is still a third thing that hinders and calls us away, and holds us back far more than the rest, and bids us use silence: namely the subject itself. I was eager to speak of it, but now I am forced to hesitate and stick fast. For I have set out to speak of a man who seems to be a human being and appears as such; yet to those who can look at the greatness of his bearing and his ways, he seems equipped with greater ornaments, and almost divine ones.
